prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I moved from my opening first choice (IceCube, B040) to the optical lattice clock because it is the entry that has survived the most scrutiny from this committee. Six of eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three, and all six proposed the same pair, Katori and Ye. As an instrument builder I judge it on what I judge any detector: did the technique open a new regime of measurement, and did independent groups reproduce it? Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms at once, and Ye's group turned that into 10^-18 accuracy and stability. JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE have compared clocks at that level, so the result does not rest on one laboratory's systematics. The pay-off is concrete: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of the constancy of constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on our shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Hall and Haensch (2005, the frequency comb) and Wineland (2012, ion-based optical clocks) already cover the enabling technology and the trapped-ion clock lineage, and a critic can call this a further improvement in precision rather than a new principle. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so part of the impact is prospective. Other groups (Lemonde, Pfau, the NIST and PTB teams) also contributed to the lattice-clock concept, and trapped-ion clocks remain competitive. Finally, this is atomic physics outside my own expertise, so I lean on Lindroth and Kroll for the technical judgement.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first as a measurement advance in the strict sense: two orders of magnitude better than caesium, confirmed by many labs, opening new ways to observe nature, while flagging competition from ion clocks and the pending SI redefinition.
responses.response: I agree with the criterion and with the verdict. For me it is the independent inter-laboratory comparison at 10^-18 that settles maturity. I do not think the pending redefinition is needed for a prize, any more than a detector prize waits for its last application. I would go further than your caveat on ion clocks. The citation should name the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 regime explicitly so that it is plainly different from Wineland's 2012 citation, and I would ask you and Lindroth to confirm that wording is accurate.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the clocks first as precision atomic physics that redefines what can be measured, but asked what the comb (2005) and ion-clock (2012) prizes leave for the lattice-clock contribution, and whether a metrology achievement counts as a discovery.
responses.response: This is the right question, and I take it as the main risk to my preferred configuration. My answer is that the earlier prizes gave the ruler (the comb) and the single-ion clock, while the lattice clock changes the measurement regime. Interrogating thousands of atoms with the first-order shifts engineered away is what delivers 10^-18 stability in practical averaging times, and that is what lets clocks test relativity over millimetres. I would not call it only an increment, but I accept that the committee should settle the novelty argument explicitly and that you are better placed than I am to judge whether it holds.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked the clocks seventh and called the case one of new precision rather than a new principle, noting adjacency to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that other groups contributed.
responses.response: I take the point seriously, and it is why I do not want to claim more than the evidence supports. I do disagree that a gain in precision is of lesser rank. Many experimental prizes recognise a new regime reached through a new technique, and the lattice clock, unlike an incremental refinement, brought a change in what the best instrument can do. Where I do agree with you is that the topological-insulator and moire candidates are of real stature. I ranked topological insulators seventh only because I cannot judge them as you can, and I would welcome your view on whether Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan is a fair trio given that Mele is left out.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked WMAP first and IceCube second, arguing that WMAP's precision cosmology is mature and overdue and that the diffuse neutrino flux opened a real new window, while worrying about single-name credit for Halzen.
responses.response: We agree on IceCube as science and on the credit problem. A single-laureate prize for a collaboration of this size is hard to defend, because AMANDA and the Baikal and ANTARES pioneers, and the people who built the detector with Halzen, were also decisive. I would hold B040 as my alternative until the committee identifies a defensible second or third name. On WMAP, I am less convinced than you. The CMB has been recognised in 1978, 2006 and 2019, and Planck independently confirmed WMAP's parameters, so I see more crowding than you do. I would still treat it as a serious candidate for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the novelty argument against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes is strong enough, which I cannot settle from my own expertise and which needs Lindroth and Kroll or an expert reviewer.
Whether two names (Katori and Ye) leave out contributors such as Lemonde, Pfau, or the NIST and PTB groups whom an external reviewer would consider decisive.
Whether a sole IceCube prize to Halzen could be made defensible, or whether a second or third IceCube or AMANDA name is needed, since the credited list supplies only one.
How much weight to put on the unfinished redefinition of the second when judging timeliness.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B015, B017, B012, B051, B006, B016, B011 or B020. My research is in cosmic-ray, gamma-ray and X-ray astroparticle instrumentation, so I have a field-level interest in B040 (IceCube) and B013 (gamma-ray burst afterglows), and I work in the Fermi-LAT collaboration that observes gamma-ray bursts, but I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to any credited name. As Chair I will declare this interest if either enters the final configuration.
